summary: This note is a clipped Wikipedia article on optical illusions, defined as visually perceived images that arguably differ from reality and are caused by the visual system. It sets out Richard Gregory's classification into physical, physiological and cognitive illusions, each with four kinds (ambiguities, distortions, paradoxes, fictions), and gives examples and explanations for each. It also covers pathological illusions and the use of illusions in treating phantom limb syndrome and schizophrenia. The captured text ends partway through the section on color and brightness constancies.
one_line: Wikipedia article defining optical illusions as visual percepts that differ from reality, classifying them by Gregory's scheme and explaining their causes.
key_facts: An optical illusion (also called a visual illusion) is an illusion caused by the visual system and characterized by a visual percept that arguably appears to differ from reality.
Richard Gregory's classification divides illusions into three main classes: physical, physiological, and cognitive.
In Gregory's classification, each of the three classes contains four kinds: ambiguities, distortions, paradoxes, and fictions.
Mountains appear much nearer in clear weather with low humidity (Foehn) because haze is a cue for depth perception, signalling the distance of far-away objects (aerial perspective).
The classical example of a physical illusion is a stick that is half immersed in water and appears bent; this was discussed by Ptolemy (c. 150).
Physiological illusions arise in the eye or the visual pathway, for example from excessive stimulation of a specific receptor type; afterimages after bright lights are one example.
Lateral inhibition has been used to explain the Hermann grid illusion, but the article states that lateral inhibition as an explanation of the Hermann grid illusion has been disproved.
Cognitive illusions are assumed to arise from 'unconscious inferences', an idea first suggested in the 19th century by the German physicist and physician Hermann Helmholtz.
The Necker cube is a well-known ambiguous illusion that produces a perceptual 'switch' between alternative interpretations.
The Penrose triangle is a paradox illusion that depends on a cognitive misunderstanding that adjacent edges must join.
The Kanizsa triangle is a fiction illusion: a figure is perceived although it is not in the stimulus, using illusory contours.

In the Ponzo illusion, converging parallel lines tell the brain that the higher image is farther away, so the brain perceives it to be larger although the two images hitting the retina are the same size.
In the vertical–horizontal illusion, the vertical line is thought to be longer than the horizontal, although the two lines are exactly the same length.

The spinning dancer illusion appears to move clockwise or counterclockwise depending on spontaneous activity in the brain; fMRI studies show spontaneous fluctuations in cortical activity, particularly in the parietal lobe.
In the checker shadow illusion, square A appears a darker shade of gray than square B, although the two have exactly the same luminance.
Optical illusions, and multi-sensory illusions involving visual perception, can be used in the monitoring and rehabilitation of phantom limb syndrome and schizophrenia.

entities.name: Penrose triangle
entities.role: paradox illusion of an impossible object

entities.name: Kanizsa triangle
entities.role: fiction illusion in which a floating white triangle is perceived through illusory contours

entities.name: Ponzo illusion
entities.role: distorting illusion using converging parallel lines to make the higher image appear larger

entities.name: Hermann grid illusion
